question: What does it mean to learn a distribution?

provenance: ES667 · chapter question

question: Where should probability mass go?

title: If we sample 100 times, what might happen?
idea: Compare the observed fractions with 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3.
provenance: ILLUSTRATIVE · seeded independent categorical draws · dashed lines = target proportions
notes: First ask for predictions with P(red)=.2, P(blue)=.5, P(green)=.3. Reveal the actual fixed-seed 100-draw histogram. Reset and use 10 draws to show fluctuation. Expected counts 20/50/30 are expectations, not guaranteed results.
question: If we sample 100 times, what might happen?
answer: Usually near 20 red, 50 blue and 30 green, with random variation.

title: What do μ and σ control?
idea: The mean moves the centre; the standard deviation changes the spread.
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT density · ILLUSTRATIVE random draws
notes: Move mean while keeping sigma fixed, then sigma while keeping mean fixed. The same standard noise is reused during parameter changes; Fresh draws changes it. Variance is sigma squared, not sigma.
question: What do μ and σ control?
answer: Mean translates the distribution; standard deviation sets its scale.

title: Is the height of this curve a probability?
idea: A point has zero probability. An interval can have positive probability.
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · standard Gaussian, rounded interval probability
notes: Reveal the interval shading. Density has units inverse to x and can exceed one. For a continuous variable the probability at a single exact value is zero. The curve is not a histogram of individual real numbers.
question: Is the height of this curve a probability?
answer: No. Integrate density over an interval to get probability.

title: Can one Gaussian describe these eight groups?
idea: The gaps matter as much as the clusters.
provenance: ILLUSTRATIVE samples · analytical mixture / moment-matched single Gaussian contours
notes: Begin with a single Gaussian matching population first and second moments. Toggle to the known mixture. Both views use the identical 280 points and axes. Eight clusters, not eight digit labels.
question: Can one Gaussian describe these eight groups?
answer: A single Gaussian cannot represent separated high-density modes with low-density gaps.

title: Could a simple recipe already generate data?
idea: Choose a centre, draw an offset, add them.
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · equal weights 1/8; radius 2.4; component σ = 0.23
notes: Use component k=0 with centre (2.4,0), and offset (0.1,-0.2), giving x=(2.5,-0.2), orally. Component labels are latent variables too. This is a real sampling recipe.
question: Could a simple recipe already generate data?
answer: Yes. A mixture is already a probability model with a precise sampling algorithm.

title: Which parameters explain our observations?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · 1D worked data: −0.5, 0.5, 1.5; fixed σ = 1
notes: Hold the observations fixed. Start at mean zero and calculate summed log density. Advance to move the mean to .25, then .5. The exact maximum is .5. Ask students whether increasing every density without preserving normalization would define a probability model. The final build introduces maximum likelihood in general.
question: Which parameters explain our observations?
answer: Choose parameters giving high likelihood to the observations. Here the best mean is .5.

title: Can we sample it? Can we evaluate its density?
idea: A sampler and a tractable density are different kinds of access.
provenance: CONCEPTUAL · sampling and tractable normalized density are separate abilities
notes: A generator can transform random samples without an easy normalized density formula. A VAE decoder likelihood is conditional; its marginal p(x) integrates over z and is usually intractable. This prepares the later GAN/flow comparison.
question: Can we sample it? Can we evaluate its density?
answer: No. Having a sampler does not imply tractable normalized density evaluation.

title: What should a neural generator do with z?

title: Could an encoder find a useful code?

title: Reconstruct a digit. Then try a prior draw.

title: How expensive is the wrong probability model?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original teaching construction
notes: Samples come from q. At each outcome compute log q minus log p, then average under q. Individual contributions may be negative; their sum is nonnegative. With q=(.8,.2), p=(.5,.5), KL=.192745 nats. Natural logs give nats. The logarithmic scoring/coding interpretation is idealized expected extra log loss.
question: How expensive is the wrong probability model?
answer: KL(q||p) is expected extra negative log probability when data drawn from q are scored using p.

title: Why does the direction of KL matter?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original teaching construction
notes: Keep q=(.8,.2), p=(.5,.5). Swapping direction changes both the log ratio and the averaging distribution. KL(q||p)=.192745; KL(p||q)=.223144. If p assigns zero mass to an event with positive q mass, KL(q||p) diverges. KL is not a symmetric distance. In VAE inference we use the q-to-posterior direction.
question: Why does the direction of KL matter?
answer: The first distribution chooses which outcomes receive weight in the average.

title: Cover both groups, or concentrate on one?

title: Can we average over a distribution we can sample?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original probability example
notes: Return to the exact three-state model. Define w(z)=p(x,z)/q(z|x), with q positive wherever the joint contributes. Multiplying each weight by q recovers the same joint contributions .02,.40,.06. Thus E_q[w]=p(x)=.48. We have changed the averaging distribution, not the model or its evidence. For continuous z the sum becomes an integral. This identity alone does not make the logarithm of that expectation easy to optimize.
question: Can we average over a distribution we can sample?
answer: Multiply and divide by q: p(x)=E_q[p(x,z)/q(z|x)]. The expectation is over the approximate posterior.

title: What changes when we move the log inside?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original probability example
notes: The weights are .05, 4/3 and .2 with averaging probabilities .4,.3,.3. First show log applied after averaging: log(.48)=-.733969. Then average the three log weights: -1.594820. The logarithm is concave, so E[log w] <= log E[w]. The lower point is the q-weighted average of the three points on the log curve; it is below the curve at the average weight. This is Jensen’s inequality. The lower expression is the Evidence Lower BOund. Equality occurs when w is constant q-almost surely, as when q is the true posterior in this toy.
question: What changes when we move the log inside?
answer: The expectation of log weights is a lower bound on the log of their expectation: ELBO <= log p(x).

title: How can we improve a bound on the evidence?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original teaching construction
notes: Exact discrete toy from the preceding evidence slide. Hold the generative model fixed, so log p(x)=log .48 is fixed. Improve q through three explicitly chosen distributions. question: How can we improve a bound on the evidence?
answer: log p(x)=ELBO+KL(q||posterior). Nonnegative KL makes ELBO a lower bound.

title: Which parts can we compute and differentiate?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original probability example
notes: For each observed x, sample z from the encoder distribution, evaluate the decoder log likelihood and subtract KL(q||prior). Approximate the reconstruction expectation with K samples; K=1 is common. Our Gaussian KL is analytic. Average the negative bound across the minibatch and update both theta and phi. The exact true-posterior KL gap is generally unavailable. Holding theta fixed tightens the bound by changing q; updating theta also changes the evidence. Improving a bound does not guarantee every stochastic update improves true marginal likelihood. Beta=1 gives this ELBO; other beta weights define a different objective. question: Which parts can we compute and differentiate?
answer: Estimate the reconstruction expectation, compute the Gaussian prior KL, and differentiate the negative bound with respect to both networks.

title: Why not optimize reconstruction alone?
section: 06 · What does the trained model learn?
idea: Reconstruct each image while keeping its posterior compatible with the prior.
provenance: ILLUSTRATIVE · authored teaching diagram
notes: Return to the measured AE mismatch. We are not adding a penalty merely for attractive scatter plots: the KL follows from the variational bound on marginal log likelihood.
question: Why not optimize reconstruction alone?
answer: Reconstruction alone does not connect the inferred latent distributions to the prior used for generation.

title: What does “reconstruction loss” actually mean?
section: 06 · What does the trained model learn?
idea: Our experiment uses binary MNIST and Bernoulli likelihood.
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · fixed threshold x > 127 applied to uint8 pixels
notes: The reconstruction term is not universally MSE. A Gaussian with fixed observation variance produces scaled squared error plus a constant. We threshold MNIST so BCE is a literal Bernoulli log likelihood, not a claim about original grayscale values.
question: What does “reconstruction loss” actually mean?
answer: It is negative log likelihood under the chosen decoder observation model.

title: What probability did we assign to these four pixels?
section: 06 · What does the trained model learn?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · four binary observations; independent Bernoulli likelihood
notes: For an observed one use p; for zero use 1-p. Multiply the four probabilities or add their negative logarithms. We sum over pixels in the MNIST experiment; a mean would divide by four here.
question: What probability did we assign to these four pixels?
answer: The sum is 1.196 nats; the mean is 0.299.

title: How far is this posterior from the prior?
section: 06 · What does the trained model learn?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · purple q(z|x), amber p(z)=N(0,1)
notes: Move mean toward zero and sigma toward one. Curve overlap is an intuition; the displayed KL uses the exact formula, not a visual area distance. KL is asymmetric and measured in nats. The second build reveals its value.
question: How far is this posterior from the prior?
answer: For these Gaussian distributions KL reaches zero exactly when mean is zero and standard deviation is one.

title: Can we calculate one KL by hand?
section: 06 · What does the trained model learn?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · natural logarithm; rounded to three decimals
notes: Substitute the mean, variance, and log variance in separate steps. Compute the bracket, then multiply by one-half. Only after that move to mu=0 and sigma=1. Equality is the minimum of this KL term alone, not a requirement that a trained VAE ignore x.
question: Can we calculate one KL by hand?
answer: About .818 nats; zero at the unit Gaussian prior.

title: Now we can assemble the VAE
section: 06 · What does the trained model learn?
idea: Reconstruction and KL both send gradients to the encoder.
provenance: ILLUSTRATIVE · authored teaching diagram
notes: This is the first full VAE architecture. The encoder produces mu and log variance, epsilon supplies independent noise, z feeds the decoder, and two loss paths supply gradients. q for each example is compared to p; this is not a class-cluster constraint.
question: Now we can assemble the VAE
answer: Every component solves a previously introduced problem: inference, differentiable sampling, observation modeling, and prior compatibility.

title: What stays when we only want a new sample?
section: 06 · What does the trained model learn?
idea: To generate, draw z from the prior and keep the decoder.
provenance: ILLUSTRATIVE · authored teaching diagram
notes: At generation time sample z from the prior. The decoder produces Bernoulli probabilities; sample each output pixel if a binary image is needed. A reconstruction instead conditions its inferred latent on x.
question: What stays when we only want a new sample?
answer: The decoder and prior suffice for generation. The encoder is used for inference and reconstruction.

title: How well do the two models reconstruct the same digits?

provenance: MEASURED · 60,000 train / 10,000 test · 15 epochs · seed 667 · unselected examples
notes: Use at most 45 seconds here. Greater latent capacity changes this run’s quality; this is not a universal benchmark. All panels are decoder probability means. Actual binary draws appeared in the opening. Held-out BCE/KL and exact architecture are in the backup and metrics manifest.
question: What did the small models actually learn?
answer: The 2D model is useful for seeing geometry; the 16D model has more capacity but still makes imperfect outputs.

title: What probability does the discriminator predict?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original probability example
notes: Define the training experiment before introducing its loss. Choose source S=1 or S=0 with equal probability. If S=1, draw x from the data distribution; otherwise draw z from the noise prior and set x=G(z). This mapping induces p_G over x even when its density is unavailable. Hide S and ask D to estimate P(S=1|x). This is source classification in a constructed mixture, not a general probability that an image is real or a density p_data(x). Equal source priors matter for the later D* formula.
question: What probability does the discriminator predict?
answer: D(x) estimates the probability that x came from the data source in this balanced classification experiment.

title: Where does the discriminator loss come from?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original probability example
notes: Use the Bernoulli conditional model P(S|x)=D(x)^S(1-D(x))^(1-S). Its log likelihood is S log D+(1-S)log(1-D). Average over the balanced source experiment. The result is V/2, where V is the sum of real and generated expectations in the original GAN objective. Multiplying by two preserves the optimum, so the implementation minimizes L_D=-V. Keep this factor explicit: an average across all real and fake examples differs by two from a sum of the two class means.
question: Where does the discriminator loss come from?
answer: The discriminator objective is ordinary binary classification log likelihood on a balanced mixture of data and generated examples.

title: What would the best discriminator say?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original probability example
notes: Use exact illustrative categorical probabilities p_data=(.6,.3,.1), p_G=(.1,.3,.6). Bayes gives D*(x)=pi p_data(x)/(pi p_data(x)+(1-pi)p_G(x)); pi is the data-source prior. At pi=.5, D*=(6/7,.5,1/7). The middle bin has score .5 even though the full distributions differ. Change pi to show why an unbalanced sampling experiment changes the posterior. Under equal priors the odds D*/(1-D*) recover the density ratio p_data/p_G. In actual GANs those densities are unavailable; D learns from samples. The formula describes the population optimum, not every trained neural discriminator.
question: What would the best discriminator say?
answer: At equal source priors, D*(x)=p_data(x)/(p_data(x)+p_G(x)); it compares the two densities at the same x.

title: How does the discriminator change as the model moves?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original probability example
notes: Original distribution diagram inspired by Goodfellow Figure 1 and Lilian Weng’s probability discussion. Here p_data=N(0,1), z~N(0,1), G_mu(z)=z+mu, so p_G=N(mu,1) is analytically known. Reveal p_G, then the exact Bayes discriminator on a separate probability axis. D*(x)=sigmoid(mu^2/2-mu*x). Move mu toward zero and inspect a fixed x. At mu=0 the distributions agree and optimal D is .5 everywhere. A trained network constantly outputting .5 could instead be underfit, so its output alone is not proof of convergence. These are controlled distributions and an oracle D*, not neural training snapshots.
question: How does the discriminator change as the model moves?
answer: The optimal discriminator follows the density ratio. When both distributions match, it cannot infer the source better than the source prior.

title: Why change the generator’s loss in practice?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original probability example
notes: Write D(G(z))=sigmoid(a), where a is the discriminator logit. For minimax generator loss log(1-D), the derivative with respect to a is -D. For non-saturating loss -log D, it is D-1. At a=-4, D=.017986, so the two derivatives are -.017986 and -.982014. Both updates try to increase the data-source logit, but the latter avoids the small loss-to-logit derivative when D confidently rejects the sample. The complete generator gradient also includes the derivative of the discriminator logit with respect to its input and of G with respect to its parameters; the new objective does not guarantee useful gradients in every setting. D parameters stay fixed during this update.
question: Why change the generator’s loss in practice?
answer: The non-saturating loss provides a larger loss-to-logit derivative when D strongly rejects a generated example.

provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · hand-chosen scores D(x)=0.9, D(G(z))=0.2
notes: Sum one real and one fake negative log probability for D. The non-saturating generator minimizes minus log D(fake). D is a classical sigmoid probability of source membership under its training problem, not a calibrated measure of objective realism. A WGAN critic has a different objective and interpretation.
question: What do these two losses ask for?
answer: D wants real scores high and fake scores low. G wants D(fake) high.

title: How is the ideal game connected to KL?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · original probability example
notes: Return to the exact three-bin distributions. Form m=(p_data+p_G)/2 and average KL(p_data||m) and KL(p_G||m): this is Jensen–Shannon divergence. Substitute the optimal discriminator into the classical minimax value to obtain V(G,D*)=-log 4+2 JS. Change the categorical model along a chosen interpolation toward the data distribution. JS reaches zero and V reaches -log 4. This is an analytical distribution path, not a learned G update. The result assumes optimal D and the original balanced minimax objective. Finite alternating updates with the non-saturating generator loss are not literally gradient descent on this JS expression.
question: How is the ideal game connected to KL?
answer: Under an optimal balanced discriminator, the classical minimax value differs from twice JS only by -log 4.

title: What if our generator were invertible?

notes: Move deformation slowly. The concrete map is x1=z1 and x2=z2+a*.6*sin(1.25*z1), which has an explicit inverse and determinant one. It illustrates invertibility, not a successful learned multimodal density. It does not equal flow matching.
question: What if our generator were invertible?
answer: We can map observations back to the base distribution and account for local volume change.

title: Where does exact density come from?
provenance: ANALYTICAL / EXACT · inverse-Jacobian convention; 1D stretch illustration
notes: The forward map x=2z doubles interval length. Its probability mass stays fixed, so density halves. The inverse derivative is one-half. This explains the plus log absolute inverse Jacobian convention. Ordinary generators need not be invertible; a VAE encoder and decoder are not generally inverses. This is normalizing flow, not flow matching.
question: Where does exact density come from?
answer: Change of variables combines the base density with the inverse map’s local volume correction.
